opus-5.5.text:
Well, I want to be careful here, because I'm not claiming it would be more capable along every dimension. A Scientist AI is deliberately not an agent. It isn't trying to achieve goals in the world, so in that sense it gives up something. But in terms of understanding, prediction, and generalization, I think there are good reasons to expect an advantage.

The main reason is the way it uses data. A standard large language model is trained to imitate: predict the next token the way a human would have written it. That means it absorbs not only our knowledge but also our confusions, our motivated reasoning, and the fact that what people say isn't always what's true. The Scientist AI is trained differently. It's trying to build a model of the world, a set of hypotheses or explanations, and to treat the data as observations generated by those underlying causes. It isn't treating the text as the truth to copy. When someone writes "X is true," the right inference is "this person said X is true," and then you ask what that tells you about the world, given who said it and why. That separation between what is said and what is the case is, I think, much more data-efficient and much more robust.

The second reason has to do with generalization. If you learn causal, compositional explanations, the kind of structured latent variables scientists use, you can combine them in new ways to handle situations you've never seen. Current models are impressive, but they still fail out of distribution in ways that suggest they're often relying on surface patterns. A system that is explicitly trained to find explanations that account for the data, and that keeps track of uncertainty over competing explanations, should extrapolate better. It's the difference between memorizing many solved exercises and actually understanding the theory.

The third point is about uncertainty itself. In the Bayesian framing I'm advocating, the system doesn't commit to one story. It keeps a distribution over theories. With amortized inference methods like the GFlowNet-style approaches we've been working on, you can train a neural net to sample explanations in proportion to how well they account for the evidence. That gives you calibrated answers, and calibration is a form of capability. Knowing when you don't know is extremely valuable, both for safety and for deciding what experiment or question would be most informative next.

And finally, there's a kind of synthetic-data advantage. Once you have a world model that can generate and evaluate hypotheses, you can essentially do your own thinking offline. You reason, check consistency, and refine explanations without needing new human-written data. Humans do this. Scientists don't just read more papers. They think, and they test whether their ideas hang together. So for the same amount of external data and compute spent on raw imitation, I'd expect a system that invests in building coherent explanations to get more out of it.

So my claim is about honesty and trustworthiness, but it's also a bet that the scientific way of learning is simply a better way to learn. And if that's right, we don't have to choose between safety and capability, at least for this class of non-agentic systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first I should say I'm not certain it will be more capable. That's not actually the main motivation — the main motivation is safety. But there are reasons to think we're not necessarily paying a big price, and we might even gain something.

The key idea is that the Scientist AI is trained to do one thing: build a good explanatory model of the world and give calibrated probabilities to statements about it. It's not trained to please you, to imitate humans, or to achieve goals in the world. And when you look at how we train current frontier systems, a lot of the compute and data goes into things that are actually in tension with being a good scientist. Imitation learning on human text teaches the model to reproduce human errors, human biases, human confidence. Reinforcement learning from human feedback teaches it to say what the rater likes, which we know produces sycophancy and overconfidence. These are forms of pressure pushing the model away from the truth.

So if you remove those pressures, and instead the training signal is just, "Is your probabilistic explanation consistent with the data? Are your predictions calibrated?" — you get a model where the inductive bias is pointed at understanding rather than at persuasion or agency. That's one reason to think you get more out of the same compute: you're not wasting capacity learning to be a convincing agent.

The second reason is more technical and has to do with how the system reasons. In the design I have in mind, the model doesn't just output an answer. It generates candidate explanations — latent hypotheses, if you like — and it treats those as random variables with probabilities. So instead of committing to one chain of thought, like current reasoning models tend to do, it's doing something closer to Bayesian inference: considering many possible explanations and weighting them. That gives you much better uncertainty estimates, and good uncertainty estimates are enormously valuable when you want to generalize, when you're in a situation the model hasn't seen before. A model that knows what it doesn't know is more useful, and in a sense more capable, than one that confidently hallucinates.

And then there's a scaling argument. A lot of the limiting factor for current systems isn't raw compute, it's the lack of a coherent world model and the lack of trustworthy reasoning. If you have a system that can do approximate probabilistic inference over explanations, you can in principle give it more compute at inference time and it gets closer to the right posterior — the right answer. That's a cleaner scaling story than "sample more chains of thought and vote."

But I want to be careful. These are arguments about the direction of the design. Whether it actually ends up ahead of a standard model on, say, coding benchmarks — I don't know, and honestly that's not the question that keeps me up at night. The question is whether we can build something very capable that doesn't have goals of its own, that is honest by construction, and that we can use as a guardrail on the agentic systems people are rushing to deploy anyway. If it turns out to be a bit less capable on some tasks but much safer, I think that's a trade worth making.

astra-6.text:
I would qualify that: I don’t think we know that it would be more capable across the board. The argument is that its training objective would be more directly aligned with discovering explanations of the data, rather than imitating the answers that humans produce.

Think about the distinction between a student who learns to reproduce solutions and a student who understands the underlying principles. Both might see the same examples, but understanding the principles can let you generalise to situations that look quite different. What we would like the Scientist AI to do is consider different hypotheses about how the world works, and assess how well they explain the observations, while retaining uncertainty when several explanations are plausible.

That could make better use of the data. A good explanation captures structure that applies to many observations, including observations you haven’t seen yet. But finding those explanations is computationally difficult. So the crucial question is whether we can develop sufficiently good approximations to that inference process within a given compute budget. I see a reason to pursue that direction, rather than a demonstrated guarantee that it will outperform a standard model with the same resources.

sol-6.1.text:
I wouldn’t claim that it would necessarily be more capable across the board. The advantage I have in mind is that we would train it to understand and predict, rather than to produce actions that get a high reward. Those are different objectives.

Think about a scientist who considers several possible explanations of the same observations. You don’t want the system to settle on one explanation just because it can tell a convincing story. You want it to represent the uncertainty: which hypotheses are consistent with the evidence, and how much support does each one have? Then, when you ask a question, it can reason using those different possibilities.

That could give us more reliable answers, especially when the evidence is incomplete. But there’s a computational challenge in doing this well. So I see it as a research hypothesis, not a guarantee that the same amount of compute and data will automatically give you a more capable system. The central motivation is to get useful scientific understanding without also training a system to pursue goals in the world.
